headline: Space is becoming accessible to everyone, not just superpowers
meta_description: Reusable rockets and commercial providers are democratizing space exploration, opening opportunities for developing nations and young people worldwide.
summary_short: Falling launch costs and new space actors are transforming who can access orbit. The UN is working to ensure all countries benefit from the expanding space economy.
body:
The space sector is undergoing a fundamental transformation. Reusable rockets, commercial launch providers and university teams are making orbit accessible to far more countries and communities than ever before. This shift means that nations without massive aerospace budgets—and young people without decades of experience—now have genuine pathways to participate in space science, satellite communications and Earth observation. The UN Office for Outer Space Affairs is actively supporting this democratization through initiatives like KiboCUBE Academy, which provides hands-on satellite development training, and Space4Youth, a competition that has sent selected young people to astronaut training at NASA Space Camp. For developing countries historically locked out of the space economy, these opportunities represent something profound: the chance to build local expertise, launch their own satellites and tap into what the global space sector is projected to become—a trillion-dollar industry by 2030.

Yet wider access brings responsibilities alongside possibilities. As more actors reach orbit, international cooperation becomes critical. The UN's Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space is now addressing complex challenges including space traffic coordination, lunar activity planning and space debris management—questions that will shape how humanity uses space for generations. The committee recently established an Expert Group on Space Situational Awareness to strengthen information-sharing between nations as orbital activity increases.

This year's World Space Week, marked annually from October 4 to 10 and now running its theme "Rocket revolution," reflects this new reality. More than 50,000 events are planned across over 100 countries, many designed to engage people who will never become astronauts but still want to participate in humanity's space endeavor.
quick_facts: Reusable rockets and commercial providers are lowering launch costs globally
KiboCUBE Academy offers satellite development training for space engineers
Space4Youth competition sends selected young people to NASA Space Camp
Over 50,000 World Space Week events planned in 100+ countries
Global space economy projected to reach one trillion dollars by 2030
